extracted.intended_audience: student editors, teachers, and judges of scholastic (school) newspapers; journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: A scoring and self-evaluation rubric for scholastic newspapers covering news values, writing and editing, editorials, headlines/typography, and production/style conventions. Intended to guide judges and editors in diagnosing strengths and weaknesses and assigning penalties/scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section maximum scores and total scoring scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall scoring is divided into major sections with maximum points: News Values and Sources (230), News Writing and Editing (800), Editorials and Entertaining Matter (180), Headlines, Typography, and Make-up (290); total maximum 1,000 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the section maxima to compute total score and then classify the paper according to the Table of Honor Grades (All-American/Superior, First Class/Excellent, Second Class/Good, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: News coverage system (organized system to cover sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there evidence that a well organized system has been developed to insure the effective covering of all news sources? Are the following major sources covered: (a) Administrative and academic offices; (b) Clubs and organizations; (c) Athletics; (d) Other activities; (e) Personal news?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks indicate chief deficiencies. Scoring guidance: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 25; Fair, penalty 50; (worse penalties for poorer ratings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of news content among sources and reader convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the news content well balanced between the various sources (e.g., athletics often overplayed)? Is it organized for the convenience of the reader? Is there something of probable interest to every reader?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 10; Fair, penalty 25; Poor: larger penalty. Consider whether coverage is reader-oriented and proportionate across beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingenuity and resourcefulness of news development
rubrics_metrics.description: Does news content indicate ingenuity and resourcefulness in the development of news sources? Is the news restricted to routine matters?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 15; Fair, penalty 30. Look for enterprise reporting, creative sourcing, and original angles rather than routine items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other news values suggestions (penalties up to 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscellaneous additional considerations for news values and content that may warrant penalties up to 30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as discretionary scoring to reflect other significant news-value deficiencies not captured elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: News writing quality (leads, organization, style, identification, concision)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the news writing good? (Checks indicate chief faults.) Subpoints: a. Are leads complete? b. Are leads awkwardly written or overburdened? c. Do leads feature distinctive elements of story? d. Are stories well organized following the lead? e. Are stories written in simple, direct style? f. Are they free from expressions of reporters' opinions? g. Are stories brightened by a variation of style (use of quotations, etc.)? h. Are persons mentioned in stories identified—first name or initials, position, or titles, etc.? i. Are stories compactly written and free from non-essentials and padding? j. Do paragraph lengths conform to best principles of newspaper writing? k. Do paragraphs open with interest-arousing words?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring examples: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 25; Fair, penalty 50; Poor, penalty 100. Use the subpoints as checklist items when assigning penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-story treatment of non-timely or striking items
rubrics_metrics.description: Are stories that are lacking timely qualities or that have striking feature elements written in the feature story style? Have the possibilities of such stories been adequately developed? Is skill displayed in the writing of these stories?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 15; Fair, penalty 30; Poor, penalty 60. Evaluate whether appropriate stories receive feature treatment and are skillfully developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports writing faults and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are sports stories free from faults: (a) Partisanship; (b) Use of slang and 'trick' writing; (c) Too few fact stories and too many 'dope' stories; (d) Too great emphasis on major sports?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 10; Fair, penalty 20; Poor, penalty 40. Assess objectivity, tone, factual emphasis, and balance across sports coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyreading and proofreading / consistent style
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there evidences of good copyreading and proofreading? Is a consistent style used for capitalization, punctuation, numerals, etc.? Are stories marred by frequently misspelled words, mistakes in grammar, trite expressions, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 20; Fair, penalty 40; Poor, larger penalty. Look for consistent house style and minimal mechanical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other writing and editing suggestions (discretionary penalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional suggestions on writing and editing for which penalties may be exacted (unspecified amount).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as discretionary penalties (text indicates 'Other suggestions... penalties up to ...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials should address real school problems (avoid generalization/scolding/irrelevance/dull headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do editorials deal with the real problems of the school or are they marked by faults: (a) Generalization and constant exhortation; (b) Frequent scolding; (c) Consideration of matters unrelated to the life and interests of the school; (d) Introduced by dull headings followed by uninteresting writing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 25; Fair, penalty 50; Poor, larger penalty. Judge editorial relevance, tone, and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of other editorial-page features
rubrics_metrics.description: Are other editorial page features of a quality that reflects credit on the school? Consider: a. Is the material of school-wide interest? b. Is it up to the standards of the rest of the paper? c. Is it matter that has local appeal? d. Is it the original work of the students?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 15; Fair, penalty 30; Poor, penalty (higher). Evaluate breadth of appeal, standards, local relevance, and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary editorial considerations (non-scored but contributory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain features are not specifically scored due to varying conditions, but can contribute: student opinion columns; use of auxiliary agencies for editorial campaigns; critical writings (book reviews), literary departments, verse, essays, fiction by students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These items should be encouraged and may affect overall judgment though not specifically scored in every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other editorial/page entertainment suggestions (penalties up to 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: Miscellaneous additional editorial suggestions for which penalties up to 20 may be exacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply discretion for additional editorial deficiencies not captured above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline content and headline-writing principles
rubrics_metrics.description: In scoring headline content consider: a. Are headlines good summaries of stories presenting the significant feature? b. Are they well balanced and mechanically attractive? c. Are they free from hyphenated words in major decks? d. Are their meanings easily grasped? e. Do they conform to the principles set forth in the discussion on headline writing?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 20; Fair, penalty 40; Poor, larger penalty. Use headline-writing principles (summary, clarity, mechanical attractiveness) when rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of subheads
rubrics_metrics.description: Are subheads properly used?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 5; Fair, penalty 10; Poor, penalty 20. Judge whether subheads break copy helpfully and are used appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographic attractiveness and appropriate use of headline/body type
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper attractive typographically? a. Are the headline type sizes and variety of headlines used suited to the size of the newspaper? b. Does practice of too few or too many styles spoil appearance? c. Do headlines as a rule contain too many decks? d. Is the headline type attractive and easy to read? e. Is body type attractive and suitable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 15; Fair, penalty 30. Evaluate typographic coherence, readability, and suitability to paper size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Front-page make-up effectiveness and avoidance of sensational practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the make-up of the front page generally effective? a. Do all stories have headlines? b. Is the page free of excessive tabulations? c. Are headlines so placed as to conform to standard make-up practices? d. Does the page avoid undesirable and sensational make-up practices? e. Is the name of the paper significant (not a puzzling tongue-twister)? f. Is the name plate typographically attractive and suitable? g. Are news and feature stories generally too long?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 15; Fair, penalty 30. Consider standard makeup practices and whether space is used sensibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attractiveness of inside pages and department presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the inside pages attractive? a. Does the editorial page have an attractive literary appearance? b. Are inside news pages made attractive by display headlines and departmental headings? c. Is advertising arranged attractively? d. Does the sport page have a lively appearance? e. Do inside and back pages carry running heads?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring: Excellent, no penalty; Good, penalty 10; Fair, penalty 20. Assess internal page design and departmental presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other headlines, typography, and make-up suggestions (penalties up to 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional discretionary suggestions on headlines, typography, and make-up for which penalties up to 30 may be exacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as catch-all for significant make-up or typographic faults not covered above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification table / grade thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Table of Honor Grades maps total scores to classifications (All-American / Superior / First Class / Excellent / Second Class / Good, etc.) with different cutoffs by frequency (daily, semi-weekly, weekly, bi-weekly/monthly) and by type of school (universities, high schools, private schools, junior high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After totaling points, use the provided thresholds to assign an overall classification. (Specific numeric thresholds and ranges are provided in the table in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead-writing principle: include only necessary facts
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a lead, combine elements into a lead and omit any detail not necessary to the lead. Use only the facts needed to fulfill the requirements of a good lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice concise, essential-lead writing; examples in the text illustrate acceptable leads and note 'other details are unnecessary.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Never use first person in a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the first person in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third-person reporting style ('said Mr. X' or 'wrote Mr. X') rather than first-person narration; this is presented as a firm stylistic rule in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and antecedent agreement (avoid incorrect 'their')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use correct grammar and antecedent agreement; the example notes 'Their is incorrect; antecedent, Association, in the singular number.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure pronouns agree in number with antecedents and avoid colloquial or incorrect forms; careful copyediting required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable spelling and style-list usage (British vs American vs Century/Standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spelling should follow the order called for (British, Century, Standard, or Webster/American). Operator should always correct obviously misspelled words. Use the provided variable spelling list where orders call for British, Century, or Standard list. For words not on the list, follow copy. Use Webster Dictionary where order calls for Webster or American spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If British spelling is ordered, apply rules consistently (use 's' instead of 'z' in words like realise; use 'our' endings like 'honour'; double 'l' in travelling, etc.). Follow copy for hyphenation except hyphenate all words with prefix 'self' (self-control). The appendix provides extensive word lists showing variants across Webster, American, British, Century, and Standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical linotype/copy operator guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators must follow the spelling/style order given and correct obvious misspellings; use the specified dictionary (Webster or other) as ordered; carry out British variations when British spelling is ordered, including with prefixes and suffixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is production-level guidance aimed at linotype operators and copy workers; follow the variable list and the rule exceptions noted in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of discretionary 'other suggestions' items
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sections include 'Other suggestions' items (news values, writing/editing, editorials, headlines/make-up) for which penalties up to specified amounts may be exacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges and editors should apply these discretionary penalties for notable deficiencies not enumerated in checklist items; amounts vary by section (examples: up to 30 in news values, up to 20 in editorials).
